title: Incident and performance forms as one system
audience: Supervisors and owners who record incidents and assess the performance of cleaning staff.
learningOutcomes: Record an incident with facts, immediate action and a follow-up date
Rate performance against defined, observable standards, with evidence
Link incident, performance and training records so that corrective action is proportionate and documented

instruction.heading: One system, several forms
instruction.body: The sample proposal includes an incident report, a performance appraisal form, an absence report and an overtime request. These work as a system because they share a person's record and a supervisor's review. An incident can lead to training. A pattern in site inspections can feed a performance review. Absence patterns can point to a rostering problem. Design the forms so that each one points to the next step, and so that a person's file can be read in order.

instruction.heading: Record incidents as facts first
instruction.body: An incident record states the date, the time, the place, the people involved, what happened, what was done straight away, whether anyone was hurt, any witnesses, and the follow-up date. Write facts before opinions, and keep the description specific. 'The mop bucket was left on the stairs at 4 pm' is usable. 'The worker was careless' is not. The sample incident form has an explanation area and a section for the level of corrective action. Complete the explanation first, and decide on any action only after the facts are recorded.

instruction.heading: Corrective action must be proportionate
instruction.body: The sample offers three levels of action: a verbal warning, a written warning, and suspension with referral to human resources. The levels exist for a reason, but each step needs a procedure and a record. For most first incidents the right response is feedback, a retraining step and a dated note. Record the response and the reason for it.

instruction.heading: Keep safety incidents separate from discipline
instruction.body: An injury, a near miss, a chemical exposure or damage to a client's property is first a safety event. It must be reported, treated and recorded under the workplace safety procedure before any discipline is considered. A disciplinary form does not replace an injury record.

instruction.heading: Rate performance against standards
instruction.body: The sample appraisal uses nine competency areas, including job knowledge, quality of work, productivity, dependability, attendance, teamwork, personal hygiene, safety awareness and supervisor ability. Each area is rated as exceeding, achieving or below standard, and where a person achieves the standard the rater adds a marginal or proficient level. Define each area in observable terms before the review. For example, quality of work should mean the checklist items completed to standard on inspected jobs, not the supervisor's general impression.

instruction.heading: Link the forms into a plan
instruction.body: A below-standard result should lead to a sequence: documented feedback, then support or retraining, then a performance improvement plan if the result does not change. The sample says that a below-standard result calls for help from the operations team. Write the improvement plan with specific actions, a named support contact and a review date. A plan without support is a warning, not an improvement plan.

instruction.heading: Handle personal and health matters carefully
instruction.body: The personal hygiene area in the sample appraisal needs particular care. Record what was observed and what was asked, in factual terms, and discuss it privately. Do not record medical diagnoses or health details unless the person has given consent and there is a confirmed reason. Store performance and health-related information securely, and limit who can read it.

procedure: Record the incident facts at the time, including the people, the place and the immediate action.
Check whether any injury or safety duty applies, and follow the safety procedure first.
Decide the corrective action after the facts are recorded, and choose the proportionate step.
Define the observable standard for each appraisal area before the review.
Complete the appraisal with evidence for each rating.
Where a standard is not met, plan support with a named contact and a review date.
Link the incident, appraisal and training records in the person's file.
Review open actions at each follow-up date and close them with a record.

workedExamples.situation: A team member has missed two site inspections this month and was involved in a near miss, in which a chemical container was left open beside a walkway. The supervisor believes the worker is careless.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which forms are used, and what action is proportionate?
workedExamples.reasoning: The near miss gets an incident record with facts and immediate action, and it is reviewed under the safety procedure. The missed inspections are recorded as facts and checked against the worker's training records and roster. The supervisor gives documented feedback, confirms the chemical storage standard, and schedules retraining. A performance improvement plan is considered only if the inspection results do not change after support. The word 'careless' is not recorded as a finding.

equipmentAndPpe: Copies of the incident, appraisal and improvement plan forms
Private meeting space for performance discussions
PPE as listed in {{business:safety.required_ppe}} when assessing a site

commonErrors.error: Using a disciplinary form in place of an injury record
commonErrors.prevention: Record injuries and near misses on the safety form first, and treat any injury before discipline is considered.

commonErrors.error: Rating performance with no defined standard
commonErrors.prevention: Write the observable standard for each area before the review.

commonErrors.error: Recording health details in an appraisal
commonErrors.prevention: Record only the observed behaviour and the agreed action. Keep health information out of the file unless consent and a confirmed reason exist.

commonErrors.error: Issuing a warning with no support or follow-up
commonErrors.prevention: Attach a support action and a review date to every corrective step.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Workplace injury and notifiable incident reporting duties apply under state and territory work health and safety laws.

Disciplinary, suspension and dismissal steps are subject to employment law, including the Fair Work Act 2009 and any applicable award or agreement. Seek advice from a qualified adviser before any suspension or dismissal.
Health information and performance records are personal information. Handle them securely and limit access.

qualityStandard: Each incident record has the facts, the people, the immediate action, a follow-up date and a status.
Each appraisal rating cites an observable standard and the evidence for it.
Any improvement plan lists the support action, a named contact and a review date.
Safety events are handled under the safety procedure before any discipline is considered.
documentationEvidence: Incident record with facts, action and follow-up
Performance appraisal with standards and evidence
Improvement plan with support and review dates
Training record linked to any retraining
summary: Record incidents as facts first, then decide the action.
Safety events go through the safety procedure before any discipline.
Rate performance against defined, observable standards.
Link incident, appraisal and training records, and start with support.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker is injured on site. Which record must be started first?
options: The incident and injury record, with the immediate action taken
The performance appraisal for the year, with the rating scores
The disciplinary warning file, opened for the supervisor
The overtime request form, signed by the client

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is the best basis for a performance rating?
options: The supervisor's general impression and the team's mood on the day
How long the person has worked for the business and their age
Observable standards defined in advance, with evidence against each
Which workers are most popular with the team and who is liked by the client

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker's quality result is below standard. What should happen first?
options: Immediate suspension from all jobs, with the reason placed on the personnel file and the job sheet
Documented feedback and support or retraining, then an improvement plan with a review date if the result does not change
Removal from the roster without a record and the worker is told only by a text message on the day after
Waiting for the annual review and no feedback or support is given in the meantime to the worker at all

officialReferences.title: Model WHS Laws: incident notification
officialReferences.covers: Safe Work Australia page, read through a summary tool. Defines a notifiable incident as a death, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident that exposes someone to serious risk. The duty falls on the person conducting a business or undertaking, who must notify the state, territory or Commonwealth WHS regulator immediately. The incident site must be preserved until an inspector arrives or directs otherwise, with listed exceptions. The page says the model WHS laws were created in 2011.

officialReferences.title: Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), Compilation No. 52
officialReferences.covers: Federal Register of Legislation compilation, read through a summary tool; only the contents and opening material were read. The contents list the National Employment Standards (Part 2-2) and modern awards (Part 2-3). This is a dated snapshot; the current position must be checked on the Register. Award coverage for a given role or employer is not yet confirmed.

officialReferences.title: Health-information handling (privacy) requirements
officialReferences.pageDate: Version 2.0, May 2025; the guide says it was updated in May 2025
officialReferences.covers: OAIC Guide to health privacy (Version 2.0, May 2025), read through a summary tool for the first 100,000 of about 137,000 characters. Explains how health service providers meet their obligations under the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles for health information, including collection, use, disclosure and access. The page shows a last-updated date (May 2025). Some chapter footers still show Version 1.0, September 2019. The guide is written for health service providers, so it supports the health-information point only for businesses that hold health information. Publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.
